items.title: Google Antigravity's /teamwork-preview lands alongside Gemini 4 Carbon's GA — a multi-agent mode that spawns a planner, specialist workers and auditors from a single prompt, gated to the $200 AI Ultra tier
items.summary: Alongside Gemini 4 Carbon's paid-API general availability on November 10 (covered in yesterday's am), Google surfaced a second product worth tracking on its own: a research preview of Antigravity's multi-agent mode, invoked with the slash command /teamwork-preview. The pattern: a user sends a single prompt, a lead agent interviews the user and plans the work, then delegates to specialist worker agents and auditor agents that run asynchronously on hours-to-days-long tasks. Access is gated to Google AI Ultra subscribers (the $200/month tier) using Antigravity 2.0, and Google's own release materials warn that a single Teamwork session can exhaust the subscriber's entire weekly quota within a couple of tasks. Reported results from Google: a security audit that identified four previously unknown critical-severity bugs by tracing runtime permissions in a target codebase, and a separate math-and-engineering demo that produced a working CPU simulator. Overnight update (Nov 11–12): Google's own 'teamwork-when-ai-becomes-a-research-partner' Antigravity blog post surfaced, and it reframes Teamwork as an active research preview — Google states it is 'rolling out these improvements to the /teamwork-preview command in Antigravity over the coming weeks,' which signals the current behavior is not the final behavior. The model-powering-Teamwork ambiguity has not resolved and has in fact gotten slightly worse: one Google post pairs Teamwork with Gemini 3.7 Flash, the Antigravity 2.0 post names Gemini 3.5 Flash with 3.5 Pro rolling out 'next month,' MindStudio's writeup (lower reliability) still names Gemini 4 Argon, and 9to5Google's Oct 15 report confirmed Argon as the general Antigravity flagship for AI Pro. Treat the underlying model as 'one of the Flash tier Gemini variants, flavor not yet pinned down,' not as a confirmed pairing. Developer feedback is starting to surface the practical rough edges — the ai.google.dev developer forum has a 'working not working?' thread about /teamwork-preview, including one complaint that a single session dumped dozens of Markdown files straight into the agent's working directory. The underlying mechanism — a multi-agent swarm coordinated by one planning agent — is still the first major-lab product to put the Scion-style testbed pattern (parallel agents with isolated identities and shared workspaces) behind a consumer-facing slash command in an IDE-adjacent surface.
items.why_it_matters: Teamwork is worth noticing even if you will not pay $200/month for it. Three reasons, with one new caveat from overnight. First, it is the first major-lab product that puts multi-agent orchestration behind a user-facing slash command in a developer-adjacent surface. Everything before this — OpenAI Swarm, LangGraph, AutoGen, CrewAI, Google's own Scion testbed — is a framework you assemble yourself. Teamwork is the first time a frontier lab has shipped the assembly as a single feature. If the pattern catches on, expect Cursor, Claude Code, Codex CLI, and the next generation of IDE plugins to carry a similar slash command within three to six months. Second, the planner-plus-workers-plus-auditors structure is worth understanding independently of the product, because it maps cleanly onto patterns Gabe can build in Python. The Agent SDK ships the hook-and-tool-call surface that would let you build a stripped-down version of this yourself: a top-level planner agent calls a worker agent for each step, and an auditor agent reviews the output. That is a small weekend project and a direct way to learn what a multi-agent loop actually costs in tokens and wall-time. Third, the quota warning is the one to carry forward. Google's own language — a single Teamwork session can exhaust the subscriber's weekly quota in a couple of tasks — is the clearest public signal yet from a frontier lab that multi-agent workloads are 10-100x the cost of a single-agent chat, and that pricing for agent workloads is going to look very different from the $20/month flat-rate pattern today. New caveat from overnight: Google's own blog language ('rolling out these improvements over the coming weeks') and the surfacing developer complaints about scratch-file sprawl are a reminder that this is a research preview, not a stable product. The practical version for Gabe stays the same — wait for a $20-tier equivalent to appear in the next 6-12 months, or build a tiny version on the Anthropic or Gemini API and measure the per-task cost yourself — but add: do not try to build a production workflow on Teamwork today, because the surface will change out from under you over the next several weeks.

items.title: Mistral Large 4 'Le Chonk' open weights have been on Hugging Face since October 29 — a 1-trillion-parameter model with 52B active, Mistral Ecosystem Open-Weight License, with Mistral's self-reported benchmarks now partially contradicted by independent leaderboards
items.summary: Mistral released the full weights of Mistral Large 4 — internally nicknamed 'Le Chonk' — on Hugging Face on October 29, 2026, under the Mistral Ecosystem Open-Weight License (a modified MIT variant). The primary repository is mistralai/Mistral-Large-4-1T-A52B, with a separate NVFP4-quantized checkpoint published alongside. The architecture: approximately 1.05 trillion total parameters with around 52 billion active per token (sources disagree between 49B and 52B active; the model card lists 52B). Natively multimodal — image and text inputs supported. Mistral's reported Terminal-Bench 4.0 score rose from 28% at preview to 41% after additional reinforcement learning, which Mistral frames as a 13-point gain between preview and open-weight release. Overnight update (Nov 11–12): independent leaderboard context has sharpened and partially contradicts Mistral's own framing. On the Artificial Analysis Coding Agent Index, Mistral claims a 48% score 'effectively tied with' GLM-5.3 while using 47% fewer tokens per task — but the broader Artificial Analysis data shows GLM-5.3 ahead of Mistral Large 4 on Terminal-Bench 4.0, AutomationBench-AA, and AA-Briefcase; Mistral's 'tie' framing is specific to the single index it chose. The strongest frontier-closed number for context: Anthropic's Mythos 5.1 is reported at 60.9% on Terminal-Bench 4.0 — about 20 points ahead of Mistral's 41%, which positions Le Chonk as a strong open-weight option rather than a frontier-parity option. A Hugging Face technical post independently lists 28.3% on Terminal-Bench 4 and 49.8% on the Coding Agent Index — the Terminal-Bench number is roughly where Mistral's preview was before the post-release RL run, which raises a question about whether the post-release improvements fully reproduce for independent evaluators or depend on specific agent scaffolding Mistral used in-house. A separate secondary report cites 19.7% on Cognition's private FrontierCode 2.0 benchmark — vendor-aggregator-reported rather than from Mistral or Cognition directly. Hardware requirements are unchanged: approximately 1 TB in FP8 precision, or approximately 580 GB in NVFP4 quantization — self-hostable only on serious GPU budgets. The licensing terms remain the most permissive among the current trillion-parameter open-weight tier: no revenue thresholds, no field-of-use restrictions, trademark retained.
items.why_it_matters: This is a catch-up item that is worth putting into the snapshot during Cursor-transition week specifically, with a sharpened read now that independent benchmarks have surfaced. Over the next 7-10 days, developer teams running Cursor are picking replacement providers — Anthropic Claude, Google Gemini, SpaceXAI Grok, or an open-weight stack. Mistral Large 4 is the strongest EU-based option in that evaluation. Three threads matter. First, the licensing structure is the one real differentiator against the Chinese open-weight stack. The Mistral Ecosystem Open-Weight License is close to MIT (no revenue thresholds, no field-of-use restrictions), which lets a hobbyist wrap the model in a side project or a commercial tool without worrying about the kind of compete-with-DeepSeek clauses that make the DeepSeek R2 license more restrictive. Second, the token-efficiency claim — 47% fewer tokens per task at equivalent coding-agent-index score — is the specific capability lane that matters for agentic workflows. Coding agents are token-bound before they are quality-bound; a model that does the same task in half the tokens is substantially cheaper at scale, and that compounds in long tool-use sequences. Updated caveat: Mistral's 'effectively tied with GLM-5.3' framing is specific to one index. On the broader AA data, GLM-5.3 is ahead on Terminal-Bench 4.0, AutomationBench-AA, and AA-Briefcase. And an independent Hugging Face technical post lists Terminal-Bench 4 at 28.3% — roughly where Mistral was before the RL improvements — which raises an honest question about whether the 13-point post-release gain is reproducing universally or is scaffolding-dependent. The practical read: Le Chonk is a strong open-weight option, but 'strongest EU-based open-weight model' is a more honest framing than 'frontier-parity.' Mythos 5.1's 60.9% on Terminal-Bench 4.0 is still roughly 20 points ahead; frontier closed models remain the capability leaders, open-weight options remain the portability-and-cost leaders. Third, the hardware constraint is the honest one: 1 TB in FP8 means self-hosting requires 10-12 top-end datacenter GPUs. The quantized checkpoint drops that to about 580 GB — still well above a consumer workstation. For Gabe, this is not a self-host candidate without a cloud rental, but it is a viable API-based option via Mistral's La Plateforme, Together AI, Fireworks, and other open-model hosts. Keeping a third viable provider configured (alongside Anthropic and Google) is a small amount of work for a significant resilience gain, as the Cursor shutoff happening today underscores.

items.title: AI Engineer Code Summit runs Nov 10-12 in San Francisco — Day 1 (Nov 11) completed without visible major lab announcements; Day 2 (Nov 12) overlaps with Cursor's OpenAI shutoff
items.summary: The AI Engineer Code Summit, the second annual edition of swyx's application-only single-track summit on coding agents, is running November 10-12, 2026 at the Hilton San Francisco Union Square. Program format: November 10 is a workshop day, and November 11-12 are two full days of single-track keynotes and sessions alongside a Summit Expo and an afterparty. The focus is explicitly coding agents, code review, and internal agents — the summit's framing is developer-tools engineers and the teams running agentic workflows in production at companies like Ramp and Coinbase. Confirmed speakers include Databricks' Ankit Mathur and Cognition co-founder Walden Yan. The broader lineup was not fully published as of this snapshot and the official schedule page notes that program details are still being assembled. Overnight update (Nov 11–12): Day 1 completed without visible major-lab product announcements timed to the summit — no new model drops, no new MCP server releases that surfaced through overnight search, no new coding-agent framework launches. This is actually useful information: it suggests the summit this year is more a venue for community pattern-sharing than for vendor product announcements, which differs from some earlier predictions. The week-long context remains dense: today (Nov 12, the summit's final day) overlaps with Cursor's OpenAI-model shutoff going into effect, which is a live transition moment the room will be discussing in the hallway track. Expect the summit's livestream, swyx's Latent Space podcast coverage, and the YouTube session uploads (on a 1–3 week lag) to be the better signal for what actually gets said. The Sessionize call-for-speakers page lists an unusual Nov 11-13 window for the event that conflicts with the Nov 10-12 window on the official ai.engineer page — treat the Nov 10-12 window as authoritative.
items.why_it_matters: This is a Tier-3 scene-setting item, now with one observation from overnight. Three things make it worth documenting. First, the Code Summit is now the single most important venue for developer-tooling announcements in the AI-coding-agent space — in a way that the AI Engineer World's Fair in June covers the broader applied-AI audience. For anyone tracking Claude Code, Cursor, Codex CLI, Devin, Aider, OpenHands, or any of the newer agentic-coding tools, the summit is where the practical patterns and the next tool releases surface. The 2025 edition in NYC produced several of the current patterns around hook-based agent guardrails and multi-model routing — the same themes Anthropic's November Claude Code release train is now productizing. Expect the 2026 Code Summit to similarly seed the patterns we will see in Cursor's post-OpenAI stack, Codex CLI's next release, and Claude Code's v2.2 series. Second, the summit's timing — overlapping with the Cursor shutoff on its final day — gives it a specific journalistic weight this year. The engineers running Cursor's migration lane, and the teams building replacement IDEs or CLI tools, are in the room together for three days during the transition. Expect the panel discussions and hallway-track exchanges to produce the next 6 months of 'how do you actually structure a coding-agent stack' guidance. Updated observation from overnight: Day 1 wrapped without the volume of product announcements that typically clusters around tier-1 developer conferences. That shifts the expected value of the summit from 'watch for new tool releases' toward 'watch for the patterns and the Latent Space podcast writeups,' which lands on a 1–2 week lag. Third, for a hobbyist, the practical version is: follow the summit's Latent Space podcast episodes (swyx runs both) over the next 7-10 days. The talks will land on YouTube on a 1-3 week lag, but the podcast coverage and swyx's own writeups will surface the key patterns immediately.
